lines.speaker: Aeacus
lines.text: Protesilaus, get off Helen! Why are you strangling her?

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: Because it's her fault I'm dead, Aeacus! I left my house half-built and made my bride a widow!

lines.speaker: Aeacus
lines.text: Then blame Menelaus. He’s the one who dragged you all to Troy over a woman.

lines.speaker: Menelaus
lines.text: Not me, my good man! If you want justice, strangle Paris. He abducted his own host's wife—a complete violation of hospitality. Honestly, you shouldn't be the only one strangling him. Every Greek and barbarian down here ought to be strangling him for the body count he caused.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: Even better point. [shouting] Paris! I am never letting go of your neck!

lines.speaker: Paris
lines.text: That's hardly fair, Protesilaus. We're in the same trade, you and I. I'm a lover too, possessed by the very same god. You know how it is—it's completely out of our hands. A spirit takes hold of you, drags you wherever it wants, and you absolutely cannot fight it.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: [pause] Good point again. If only I could get my hands on Eros.

lines.speaker: Aeacus
lines.text: I'll take Eros's case for him, shall I? He'd probably admit he was responsible for Paris falling in love. But as for your death? That's entirely on you, Protesilaus. The minute your ship hit the beach at Troy, you completely forgot about that poor bride of yours. You were so utterly in love with glory that you took a suicidal leap right off the front of the boat just to be the first one ashore. Which is exactly why you were the first one killed.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: Well, then I'll take my own case, Aeacus, and offer a much better defense. I wasn't responsible for that either! It was Fate. It was the threads spun for me from the very beginning.

lines.speaker: Aeacus
lines.text: [sighs] Exactly. So why are you blaming them?
